Chapter 197: Anticonvulsants

Anticonvulsant overdose is not one disease. The ED move is to sort the patient into sedative-hypnotic depression, sodium-channel blockade, hyperammonemic valproate toxicity, or delayed absorption that needs serial exams, ECGs, and levels.

Overview: Sort By Syndrome

Start with ABCs, glucose, ECG, and a drug-level strategy. Clinical status wins over a single serum level: coma, respiratory depression, seizures, QRS widening, shock, and rising levels drive disposition. Older drugs have better-defined level/toxicity relationships; newer drugs are often supportive-care cases but still have dangerous exceptions.

First generation. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, phenobarbital, primidone, and ethosuximide have classic kinetics and testable complications.
Newer agents. Lamotrigine can widen QRS/QT; topiramate can cause metabolic acidosis; tiagabine can cause seizures/coma.
Rosen source check
Rosen supports seizure/status framing.

Rosen seizure and coma chapters reinforce benzodiazepine-first seizure care and broad coma differential. Tintinalli Ch197 remains the toxicity spine for drug-specific kinetics, levels, and antidotal choices.

Phenytoin and Fosphenytoin

Phenytoin toxicity is mostly cerebellar and vestibular: nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria, tremor, and confusion. Severe coma or seizures are unusual but possible with high levels or mixed ingestion. Because phenytoin is highly protein bound, a patient with renal failure, hypoalbuminemia, malnutrition, pregnancy, burns, or cirrhosis may be toxic despite a deceptively ordinary total level.

Metabolism becomes capacity-limited; small dose changes can create disproportionate level increases. After overdose, absorption can be slow, so serial levels matter. IV phenytoin adds formulation/infusion risk: hypotension, bradycardia, conduction delay, ventricular dysrhythmia, and soft-tissue injury. Fosphenytoin is less irritating but still requires monitoring.

Carbamazepine

Carbamazepine behaves like a mixed anticholinergic plus sodium-channel blocker. Delayed absorption and ileus can cause a crescendo-decrescendo course, so one early level is not enough. Watch for CNS depression, ataxia, nystagmus, ileus, hyperreflexia, dystonia, seizures, coma, QRS widening, and dysrhythmia.

A false-positive TCA screen is a classic trap. If QRS widens, treat the ECG as sodium-channel blockade and give sodium bicarbonate. Severe cases need poison center/toxicology input for multidose activated charcoal or enhanced elimination.

Rosen vs Tintinalli
ECG-directed seizure/shock management aligns.

Rosen gives the general emergency frame for seizure and coma stabilization; Tintinalli supplies carbamazepine-specific delayed absorption, false TCA screen, serial levels, and bicarbonate trigger.

Valproic Acid / Valproate

The dangerous valproate pattern is CNS depression plus hyperammonemia, sometimes with cerebral edema, hepatotoxicity, shock, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypernatremia, hypophosphatemia, anion gap metabolic acidosis, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, lactate elevation, or delayed peaks from enteric-coated/controlled-release products.

Trend valproate level, ammonia, LFTs, glucose, electrolytes, acid-base status, platelets, lactate, and mental status. Consider L-carnitine for lethargy, coma, hyperammonemia, or hepatic dysfunction. Dialysis/extracorporeal removal is reserved for severe cases such as coma, shock, cerebral edema, severe acidosis, very high levels, or failure to improve.

Second- and Third-Generation Agents

Most isolated newer-agent overdoses are less dramatic, but they are not automatically safe. Lamotrigine can cause drowsiness, vomiting, ataxia, QRS widening, QT prolongation, seizures, status epilepticus, coma, and dysrhythmias. Topiramate can cause somnolence, agitation, seizures/status epilepticus, and metabolic acidosis. Levetiracetam, gabapentin, and pregabalin are often supportive-care CNS depression cases, worse with renal disease or sedative coingestion.

Diagnosis and Monitoring

Always early. ABCs, glucose, ECG, acetaminophen/salicylate if intentional or unclear, pregnancy test when relevant, and continuous monitoring when symptomatic.
Levels. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, and phenobarbital levels help when trended; use free phenytoin when binding is unreliable.
Valproate labs. Ammonia, LFTs, electrolytes, lactate/acid-base, glucose, platelets, calcium/phosphate.

Treatment Framework

Treat the patient first: airway, ventilation, oxygenation, fluids, vasopressors when needed, glucose correction, and electrolyte repair. Seizures get benzodiazepines first, then status epilepticus escalation. QRS widening from carbamazepine or lamotrigine-like sodium-channel blockade gets sodium bicarbonate boluses.

InterventionTypical adult doseUse
Activated charcoal50 g PO/NG onceEarly ingestion with protected airway.
Multidose charcoal25-50 g PO/NG q4hConsider for carbamazepine/phenobarbital with toxicology input.
Sodium bicarbonate1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus, repeat to narrow QRSSodium-channel blockade with QRS widening.
L-carnitine100 mg/kg IV load, max 6 g; then 50 mg/kg IV q8h, max 3 g/doseSevere valproate toxicity with coma, lethargy, hyperammonemia, or liver injury.
BenzodiazepineLorazepam 2-4 mg IV, repeat as neededSeizures/status epilepticus.
